tldr: Janssen opens Devoxx Belgium 2026 with a dancing humanoid robot, argues developers are becoming builders, weighs token costs against local models, and hosts a live Groma.md multi-agent demo.
summary: A scripted humanoid robot 'from the year 2200' opens the keynote and dances; Thomas, whose team brought it from Germany, says it was trained with reinforcement learning and NVIDIA SONIC, costs about 40,000 euros, and is the subject of their lunch talk. Stephan Janssen describes AI as both exciting and frightening: overnight he turned his non-developer son's wine spreadsheet into a Firebase-hosted website without touching code, which is why Devoxx now speaks of 'builders'. He lists the stages from copy-paste prompting through context, agentic, harness and loop engineering to 'decision engineering', where decision APIs return probabilities over constrained JSON options, useful for picking tools or flagging risky tool calls. He said OpenAI and Ollama recently shipped such APIs and that Spring AI and LangChain4j support them. He also says he has not written code himself since July 2025, and calls this year's Java track, staffed by many Oracle engineers, the best ever.

On economics, about 70% of the room uses a Claude or Codex subscription, which Janssen calls heavily subsidised, so he urges trying local models, which he puts roughly a year behind the frontier, naming Qwen and Mistral's new open-weight release. DevoxxGenie, his open-source Java IDE plugin for local models, has passed 100,000 downloads, though he now mostly works in CLIs and reviews in IntelliJ. Alex Gavrilescu, creator of Backlog.md, then demos Groma.md, which keeps a live architecture map of a codebase: six agents implement six DevoxxGenie GitHub issues as components appear on the map, followed by an architecture-level diff. A run costs $60 to over $100 in tokens versus an estimated five days of manual work. Janssen closes with the robot games competition, a reminder to rate talks, and a call to embrace the change.
keyPoints: Janssen sees natural language as the new abstraction layer and calls himself language-agnostic now, while still insisting on human code review in domains like hospitals or nuclear plants.
'Decision engineering': decision APIs take a constrained JSON set of options and return probabilities, which Janssen suggests for tool selection and judging whether a tool call is disruptive.
In Janssen's view, $100 subscriptions yield thousands of dollars of tokens a month, so prices may rise; local open-weight models are the hedge, and he says Qwen already works well as an orchestrator.

Groma.md (open source, MIT) maintains a continuously updated architecture diagram, shows parallel agents' changes on it live, and offers architecture diffs (added, modified, removed components) next to code diffs, using language-specific scanners that run offline.
Six parallel agents on a fast OpenAI model cost about $60 per rehearsal run and over $100 for the full run, against Gavrilescu's estimate of five days of manual work.
takeaways: Install a capable local model and try it as an agent orchestrator so you have an option if subscription prices rise.
Look at spec-driven tooling such as Backlog.md and architecture-level views such as Groma.md to review agent output above the line-diff level.
Rate talks in the Devoxx mobile app so speakers get feedback.

quotes.text: We are all transitioning into builders. The new abstraction layer is not programming anymore or programming languages. It's the natural language.
$120, it would have taken me manually probably five days to implement. I am more expensive than $120.

watchIf: You want the opening mood of Devoxx 2026 in 25 minutes, including a dancing robot and a live multi-agent architecture-map demo.
